\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

All numbers are on the held-out, work-disjoint test split
(\nTest{} passages).  Chance is \chanceAcc{}.

\input{tables/results_main}

\begin{figure}[H]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/ablation.png}
  \caption{Every configuration on the same test split.  Bars are accuracy and
  macro-$F_1$; the dashed line is chance.}
\end{figure}

Three results stand out, and none of them is the one we expected going in.

\subsection{The generative paradigm wins}

\begin{keybox}[title=Finding 1 --- the simpler paradigm is the stronger one]
The generative character \CharOrder-gram attributor reaches \textbf{\genCharAcc{}}
(macro-$F_1$ \genCharFone{}), beating \emph{every} discriminative
configuration --- including fine-tuned BanglaBERT at \bertFTAcc{} and the full
stylometric SVM at \svmAllAcc{}.
\end{keybox}

This inverts the usual expectation.  A generative model is trained under a
handicap: each author's language model sees only that author's text and is
never told what the others look like, whereas the discriminative models are
optimised directly on the decision boundary.  Three things appear to be
happening.

\emph{The generative model uses the whole passage.}  A Kneser--Ney character
model scores every one of the ${\sim}1{,}200$ characters in a passage and sums
the evidence.  The SVM compresses the same passage into a few thousand feature
counts first, and information not preserved by that projection is gone.

\emph{Character models suit suffixal morphology.}  The word-level generative
model scores \genWordAcc{} --- \emph{six points worse} than the character model
on identical data.  The gap is the concrete cost of not seeing inside the word
in a language where register and case live in the suffix.

\emph{The discriminative models are data-starved, and the transformer most of
all.}  \nTrain{} training passages is a lot for a 29-dimensional feature vector
and very little for a 110-million-parameter encoder.

\subsection{Twenty-nine interpretable numbers beat a transformer}

\begin{keybox}[title=Finding 2 --- feature complexity is not what carries this task]
The \textbf{structural} block alone --- 29 hand-designed scalars: sentence-length
moments, lexical richness, punctuation rates, the sadhu/chalit ratio --- scores
\textbf{\svmStructAcc{}}.  That is above 3\,000 character $n$-grams
(\svmCharAcc{}), above frozen BanglaBERT (\svmBertAcc{}), and above fine-tuned
BanglaBERT (\bertFTAcc{}).
\end{keybox}

Adding the other three families to the structural block does not help:
all-stylometric scores \svmAllAcc{}, marginally \emph{below} structural alone,
though the bootstrap intervals overlap heavily and the difference should be
read as ``no gain'', not as ``harm''.  Function words alone reach
\svmFuncAcc{}; POS $n$-grams alone \svmPosAcc{}, comfortably above chance but
the weakest family, consistent with a tagger that is right \posAcc{} of the
time.

\subsection{Pretrained versus from scratch}

On downstream accuracy the two regimes are a near-tie: frozen BanglaBERT
\svmBertAcc{} against from-scratch skip-gram \svmScratchSifAcc{} (SIF-pooled)
and \svmScratchMeanAcc{} (mean-pooled).  Nothing separates them.

The representation-level diagnostic does separate them, and in the direction
the proposal hypothesised.

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
Representation & Silhouette by \textbf{author} & by \textbf{work} & ratio \\
\midrule
Scratch skip-gram (SIF pooled)  & \silScratchSifAuthor{}  & \silScratchSifWork{}  & \silScratchSifRatio{} \\
Scratch skip-gram (mean pooled) & \silScratchMeanAuthor{} & \silScratchMeanWork{} & \silScratchMeanRatio{} \\
Frozen BanglaBERT               & \silBertAuthor{}        & \silBertWork{}        & \silBertRatio{} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\begin{keybox}[title=Finding 3 --- from-scratch embeddings hold more style per unit of topic]
Trained on \nTrain{} passages of one corpus, the from-scratch skip-gram
separates \emph{authors} nearly twice as well as frozen BanglaBERT
(\silScratchSifAuthor{} against \silBertAuthor{}), and its style-to-topic ratio
is higher (\silScratchSifRatio{} against \silBertRatio{}).  A hundred-thousand-fold
advantage in pretraining data does not transfer to this task.
\end{keybox}

Two caveats keep this honest.  First, \textbf{every ratio is below 1}: all three
representations separate individual books better than they separate authors.
Embedding-space clustering is still substantially topical, whichever way it was
obtained --- which is precisely why the work-disjoint split matters.  Second,
BanglaBERT was pretrained on modern Bangla, and this corpus is 19th-century
literary prose in a register that pretraining data barely contains.  The result
is evidence about \emph{this} domain gap, not a general verdict on pretraining.

\begin{figure}[H]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.72\linewidth]{figures/style_vs_topic.png}
  \caption{Author separation against work separation, on the same test vectors.
  A representation encoding style should have the dark bar close to the light
  one; all three fall short, and BanglaBERT falls shortest in absolute terms.}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[H]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/embedding_pca.png}
  \caption{Test passages in each embedding space, first two principal
  components.  Illustrative only --- PCA discards most of the variance --- but
  the from-scratch spaces visibly separate more authors than the frozen
  transformer does.}
\end{figure}

\subsection{The two paradigms fail differently}

They agree on \paradigmAgreement{} of test passages.  Where they disagree, the
generative model is right more often (\genOnlyCorrect{} passages against
\discOnlyCorrect{}), and on only \bothWrong{} passages are both wrong together.

More interesting is \emph{which} authors each confuses, because the answer is
not the same.

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
& Generative char-\CharOrder-gram & SVM, all stylometric \\
\midrule
Worst pair  & Bankim $\leftrightarrow$ R. Tagore (19.4\,\%)
            & R. Tagore $\leftrightarrow$ Vidyasagar (31.1\,\%) \\
Second      & Sarat $\leftrightarrow$ R. Tagore (16.9\,\%)
            & Bankim $\leftrightarrow$ Sarat (7.2\,\%) \\
R.\ Tagore $\leftrightarrow$ Vidyasagar
            & 2.4\,\% & 31.1\,\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The discriminative model's dominant error --- Tagore read as Vidyasagar, 36\,\%
of his test passages --- is one the generative model almost never makes (2\,\%).
The reason is visible in the fingerprints (§\ref{sec:interp}): Tagore and
Vidyasagar sit on the same side of the \emph{aggregate} structural axes the SVM
reads (both sadhu-leaning at $+0.31$ and $+0.65$ standard deviations, both
long-worded at $+0.54$ and $+0.60$), while their character-level texture is
quite distinct.

The generative model's characteristic failure is the opposite shape: it
\emph{over-predicts} Tagore.  His own recall is fine (0.83), but a quarter of
Bankim's passages and a third of Sarat's are pulled into his model.  Tagore
contributes 14 works spanning essays, fiction and lectures --- by far the most
heterogeneous training material of any author here --- so his language model is
the broadest and highest-entropy of the five, and a broad model wins ambiguous
passages by not being surprised by anything.  This is a known failure mode of
per-author likelihood attribution, and it is the price of the same breadth that
makes the paradigm robust on short passages.

\begin{figure}[H]
  \centering
  \begin{subfigure}{0.49\linewidth}
    \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/confusion_generative.png}
    \caption{Generative char-\CharOrder-gram LM}
  \end{subfigure}\hfill
  \begin{subfigure}{0.49\linewidth}
    \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/confusion_discriminative.png}
    \caption{Discriminative SVM, all stylometric}
  \end{subfigure}
  \caption{Row-normalised confusion.  The two paradigms make structurally
  different mistakes, which is the more useful finding than either accuracy
  alone.}
\end{figure}

\subsection{How much text is needed}

Truncating test passages and re-attributing gives the answer a user of the
interface actually wants.

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
Passage length & Generative & Discriminative \\
\midrule
\lenShort{} tokens  & \accShortGen{} & \accShortDisc{} \\
\lenLong{} tokens   & \accLongGen{}  & \accLongDisc{}  \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The generative model degrades far more gracefully.  At \lenShort{} tokens it
still scores \accShortGen{} while the SVM has fallen to \accShortDisc{} --- and
the reason is structural, not incidental: sentence-length moments and lexical
richness are \emph{distributional} statistics, and a 40-token sample gives you
two or three sentences to estimate them from.  A character model has 200-odd
characters to work with either way.

\begin{figure}[H]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.68\linewidth]{figures/length_curve.png}
  \caption{Accuracy against the amount of text supplied.  The interface warns
  the user below 80 tokens for this reason.}
\end{figure}

\section{Interpretability and style fingerprints}
\label{sec:interp}

\subsection{Which families carry the model}

Permutation importance on the combined SVM says character $n$-grams dominate
(\permCharDrop{} accuracy lost when shuffled) with everything else near zero:
POS $n$-grams \permPosDrop{}, function words \permFuncDrop{}, structural
\permStructDrop{}.

That reading would be wrong, and the ablation table is what shows why.
Structural features \emph{alone} score \svmStructAcc{} --- better than character
$n$-grams alone.  Permutation importance measures what a family contributes
\emph{given the others}, so when two families encode overlapping information the
larger one absorbs the credit and the smaller one measures as worthless.  The
two diagnostics answer different questions, and quoting only the first would
misrepresent the model.

\begin{figure}[H]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.68\linewidth]{figures/permutation_importance.png}
  \caption{Grouped permutation importance.  Read alongside the ablation table,
  not instead of it: this measures marginal contribution under redundancy.}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Style fingerprints}

Each author's mean structural feature, in corpus standard deviations.  The
register axis behaves exactly as literary history says it should:
\textbf{\mostSadhu{}} sits furthest towards sadhu, \textbf{\mostChalit{}}
furthest towards chalit.  Vidyasagar is the canonical sadhu prose stylist of the
19th century; Abanindranath Tagore, writing art criticism and children's prose
half a century later, is the most colloquial voice in the set.  Neither fact was
supplied to the model.

\begin{figure}[H]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.94\linewidth]{figures/fingerprints.png}
  \caption{Structural fingerprints, per author, in standard deviations from the
  corpus mean.  The leftmost column is the sadhu/chalit register ratio.}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Auditing a single prediction}

For a linear SVM the arithmetic behind one decision is exactly $w\cdot x + b$,
so feature $i$ contributes exactly $w_{c,i}\,x_i$ --- the same quantity SHAP
estimates for a linear model, computed rather than sampled.  The interface
reports two rankings from that decomposition: the strongest contributions
overall, and the strongest contributions \emph{restricted to families a reader
can verify by eye}.  The second list exists because character $n$-grams take
almost every top slot, and ``the trigram \bn{ায়ে}'' is not something a reader can
check against the passage the way ``this text is in the sadhu register'' is.

The generative side explains itself differently: per-character log-odds between
the winning author's model and the runner-up's, aggregated by symbol.

\section{The interface}

\begin{plainbox}
\small\ttfamily
\$ python app.py -{}-text "\bn{...বাংলা অনুচ্ছেদ...}"\\[4pt]
PREDICTED AUTHOR : Rabindranath Tagore (\bn{রবীন্দ্রনাথ ঠাকুর})\\
passage \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ : 26 tokens, 2 sentences\\
\ \ ! short passage --- estimates are noisy below about 80 tokens\\[4pt]
DISCRIMINATIVE (linear SVM over stylometric features)\\
\ \ predicted : Rabindranath Tagore\\
\ \ runner-up : Sarat Chandra Chattopadhyay \ (margin 0.386)\\
\ \ strongest evidence you can check by eye:\\
\ \ \ \ +0.0513 \ POS pattern PRON--PART\\
\ \ \ \ +0.0374 \ function word "\bn{তাহা}"\\
\ \ \ \ +0.0314 \ function word "\bn{যাহা}"\\[4pt]
GENERATIVE (per-author character n-gram language models)\\
\ \ perplexity (lower = better fit):\\
\ \ \ \ Rabindranath Tagore \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ 6.011 \ <-- best\\
\ \ \ \ Sarat Chandra Chattopadhyay \ \ \ 6.158\\
\ \ \ \ Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar \ \ \ \ \ 8.664\\[4pt]
BOTH PARADIGMS AGREE.
\end{plainbox}

Both attributors are consulted deliberately.  When they agree the answer is
worth more than either alone; when they disagree the interface says so rather
than picking a winner silently, and the disagreement is itself diagnostic ---
it usually means the passage is short or the two candidates share a register.
Notebook 06 provides the same thing with a text box.

\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limits}

\textbf{Five authors, closed set.}  The system assumes the true author is among
the five.  It has no ``none of the above''.  Three crawled candidates were
dropped for having too few works to split honestly, which shrank the study but
was the right call.

\textbf{Prose only, and that was accidental.}  Verse falls out of the
line-length filter rather than by design.  It happens to be the correct control,
but it was not a decision --- it was a side effect noticed after the fact, and
is reported as such.

\textbf{One source.}  All text is Wikisource transcriptions of specific printed
editions.  Editorial normalisation --- a publisher's house style for
punctuation or spelling --- is inside the ``style'' being measured and cannot be
separated from the author's own.

\textbf{The POS tagger is \posAcc{} accurate, and coarse.}  It folds \texttt{AUX}
into \texttt{VERB}, \texttt{PROPN} into \texttt{NOUN} and \texttt{SCONJ} into
\texttt{CCONJ}.  POS $n$-grams are correspondingly the weakest feature family;
a better tagger would likely raise \svmPosAcc{}, though how much is unknown.

\textbf{The fine-tuned transformer is compute-constrained.}  \FTEpochs{} epochs
at \FTMaxLen{} tokens on CPU, about 40 minutes.  Its \bertFTAcc{} is a lower
bound; a longer schedule on a GPU, with 512-token inputs, would likely do
better.  What the comparison licenses is ``a transformer did not beat 29 hand-designed
scalars \emph{at this budget}'' --- not ``transformers cannot win this task''.

\textbf{Character $n$-grams may still carry topic.}  A character 4-gram can
fragment a proper noun.  Work-disjoint splitting limits the damage but does not
eliminate it, since an author's recurring vocabulary spans their books.

% ===========================================================================
\section{Conclusion}

On a \nAuthors{}-author, work-disjoint Bangla prose benchmark of \nPassages{}
passages, the answers to the proposal's three questions are:

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.5em]
  \item \textbf{Generative beats discriminative.}  Per-author Kneser--Ney
        character models reach \genCharAcc{}, above every discriminative
        configuration including a fine-tuned transformer, and they degrade far
        more gracefully on short passages (\accShortGen{} against
        \accShortDisc{} at \lenShort{} tokens).
  \item \textbf{From-scratch embeddings hold more style per unit of topic.}
        They separate authors nearly twice as well as frozen BanglaBERT
        (\silScratchSifAuthor{} against \silBertAuthor{}) at a
        hundred-thousand-fold data disadvantage --- though every representation
        we measured still separates books better than authors.
  \item \textbf{Interpretable features are competitive, not a consolation
        prize.}  Twenty-nine structural scalars score \svmStructAcc{}, above
        both frozen and fine-tuned BanglaBERT, and they come with an
        explanation attached.
\end{enumerate}

The result we did not set out to find is the one we would emphasise to anyone
building on this.  \textbf{Work-disjoint splitting costs \leakGap{} of apparent
accuracy} --- \randomSplitAcc{} against \workSplitAcc{} for an identical model on
identical text.  A Bangla authorship-attribution accuracy reported without
stating which regime produced it is not interpretable, and the difference is
larger than the gap between any two systems in our results table.

\section{Reproducing this}

\begin{plainbox}
\small\ttfamily
python -m venv .venv\\
.venv/Scripts/python.exe -m pip install -r requirements.txt\\
.venv/Scripts/python.exe -m ipykernel install -{}-user -{}-name banglastylo\\[4pt]
.venv/Scripts/python.exe scripts/01\_build\_corpus.py \ \ \# \textasciitilde40 min, cached\\
.venv/Scripts/python.exe scripts/run\_notebooks.py \ \ \ \ \# \textasciitilde50 min\\
.venv/Scripts/python.exe scripts/make\_report.py\\
cd reports \&\& latexmk -xelatex report.tex
\end{plainbox}

Seed \Seed{} throughout.  Every Wikisource API response is cached under
\texttt{data/raw/cache}, so the corpus rebuilds byte-for-byte.  Every number in
this document is generated into \texttt{reports/numbers.tex} by
\texttt{scripts/make\_report.py} from the run's artifacts; none is typed by hand.

\subsection*{Environment notes}

Python 3.14, CPU only.  \texttt{gensim} and \texttt{bnlp-toolkit} have no wheel
for this Python and require a C toolchain that was unavailable, so word2vec
(\S\ref{sec:embeddings}) and the Bangla POS tagger (\S\ref{sec:tagger}) are
implemented from scratch in \texttt{src/banglastylo/}.
